thread.old_title: The rich man and Lazaros — Sheol with its divisions, and *they have Mosheh and the prophets*
thread.title: The rich man and Lazarus — Abraham's bosom, the torment, the great gulf, and *they have Moses and the prophets*
thread.old_summary: Lazaros, full of sores and laid at the gate with the dogs licking him, dies and *was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried;* (Luke 16:22). *And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.* (Luke 16:23). The dead in this parable remember, the rich man knows he has five brothers; they see, across a gulf; they are still themselves, Lazaros still Lazaros and the rich man still the rich man. And the two places are divided: *And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.* (Luke 16:26). Two inherited teachings both stumble here. The one that says the dead sleep without knowing anything has to explain away a conversation. The one that says the torment is the final and eternal state has to ignore that this is Sheol before the resurrection, a holding place and not a verdict. Enoch was shown the holding place and told how it is arranged: *And he answered me and said unto me: ‘These three have been made that the spirits of the dead might be separated. And such a division has been made for the spirits of the righteous, in which there is the bright spring of water.* (1 Enoch 22:9). *And such has been made for sinners when they die and are buried in the earth and judgement has not been executed on them in their lifetime.* (1 Enoch 22:10). *Here their spirits shall be set apart in this great pain till the great day of judgement and punishment and torment of those who curse for ever and retribution for their spirits. There He shall bind them for ever.* (1 Enoch 22:11). Awake, divided, and waiting for the great day: that is what the rich man is doing, and the parable only makes sense if that is where he is. Then the parable turns to the living. The rich man wants a messenger sent to his brothers, and Abraham answers, *they have Mosheh (Moses) and the prophets; let them hear them. If they hear not Mosheh (Moses) and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead* (Luke 16:29, 31). That is the King's standing test against every gospel that sets the Torah aside, and it was proved in the open when another Lazaros was raised at John 11 and the chief priests set about killing him. Five brothers, the leadership of the house of Yahudah (Judah), who would not hear Moses, and so did not believe when one rose.
thread.summary:
It ain't new. Luke tells it in his own words, and the words are enough:

*And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried;* (Luke 16:22)

*And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.* (Luke 16:23)

*And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.* (Luke 16:26)

Abraham's bosom on one side, torments on the other, a great gulf fixed between, and both men awake. The rich man sees, speaks, remembers his five brothers, feels the flame and asks for water. Lazarus is comforted. Abraham answers. Two teachings handed down both have to argue with the page. The one that says the dead know nothing until the resurrection has a dead man holding a conversation. The one that says this flame is the final judgment has Abraham say *now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.* (Luke 16:25) while the five brothers are still alive on the earth and no one has risen. Luke says bosom, torments, gulf, and a man waiting; he does not say the end has come. David had said the grave gives back: *But Elohim (God) will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. Selah.* (Psalm 49:15)

Then the parable turns to the living:

*Abraham saith unto him, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.* (Luke 16:29)

*And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.* (Luke 16:31)

That is the test he leaves standing against every gospel that sets Moses aside, and it was tried in the open. Another Lazarus did rise, *he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.* (John 11:43), and *the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death;* (John 12:10). Men who would not hear Moses were not persuaded by one risen from the dead, exactly as Abraham had said. *For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.* (John 5:46)
